headline: Super contributions likely outperform mortgage repayment for investors with a growth risk profile, though access, tax rate, risk tolerance and interest rates all matter
reasoning: Roger Perrett argues that for most people with surplus cash, the historical returns from superannuation on a growth or balanced-growth risk profile are likely to outperform the benefit of paying down a mortgage. He notes that the decision depends heavily on accessibility (younger investors may prefer liquidity outside super), the individual's marginal tax rate, their risk appetite, and the prevailing interest rate environment. He recommends seeking personal advice given the complexity, but frames super contributions as the likely winner on a long-term historical basis.
quote: I think like we said, there's a few things to consider. There's access, there's the tax rates that you're on, the risk that you're happy to take and the big unknown as well as their interest rates. So it's always good to get advice. But I think based on a sort of a growth risk profile or balance the growth risk profile, you can see their history showing us that you may be far better off putting it into super rather than paying it off your mortgage.
episode_title: Smash debt or stack super? | the advisory

headline: Super contributions have outperformed mortgage repayments on an after-tax basis across every measured time period over the last 10 years, though outcome depends on interest rate environment, growth profile, and individual time horizon
reasoning: Roger Perrett presents data showing that returns from one of Australia's largest super funds have exceeded home loan interest rates (which ranged from ~2.6% to ~6.25% over 10 years) on an after-tax basis across 10-year, 5-year and shorter timeframes. He notes the advantage widens further when debt is investment-related and tax-deductible, effectively reducing a 6.25% rate to around 3% for someone on the top marginal rate of 47%. However, he cautions that the outcome is not guaranteed and depends on the growth/risk profile of investments and the interest rate environment. Accessibility is also a key consideration — younger Australians face a very long wait to access super, whereas older Australians are closer to preservation age and may benefit more from directing surplus cash there.
quote: So what I've done here on on the slide is the, the, I guess the bars in orange are performance of one of the largest super funds in Australia and you can see they're on the far left. That's 10 years return, five years, et cetera. So that's throwing the, the return that I think a lot of people probably would have expected or received over the last 10 years. And what I've done in the horizontal, I guess grey area is I've sort of overlaid interest rates, the average home loan rates, not RBA rates, the actual home loan rates over the last 10 years as well... what you can see there is the orange bars of super is popping up over the top of the, the, the returns of super are actually higher than the range of interest rates that we've had over that same... you can see over every single time period in this example is that if you decided to put money into super, you would have got a better return that exceeded your interest, the interest rates on your home loan. And both of these numbers are considered after tax.
episode_title: Smash debt or stack super? | the advisory
